## Religious vows: poverty, chastity and obedience, a path of total love

**For the love of Christ, many men and women in the Church leave everything.** Not out of contempt for the world, but out of love for the coming Kingdom. In a time marked by the pursuit of pleasure, wealth and personal autonomy, religious vows are a **prophetic light** that shows another way of living: that of **Jesus poor, chaste and obedient**.

### What is a vow?

A _vow_ is a **promise made to God**. It is not a mere human resolution, but a sacred commitment by which a person gives themselves to the Lord with their whole being. The **Code of Canon Law** defines it as a “free and deliberate promise made to God of some possible and better good” (cf. c. 1191).

Among all vows, **religious vows** stand out, by which members of institutes of consecrated life solemnly commit to live the _evangelical counsels_: **poverty, chastity and obedience**. These are not mere renunciations, but **ways of loving more and better**, reproducing in one’s own life the very style of Jesus Christ.

> “By means of the vows of poverty, chastity and obedience, you can be bearers of light for the women and men of our time.”  
> — _Pope Francis, World Day for Consecrated Life_

* * *

### ✨ The vow of chastity: to love with an undivided heart

Canon 599 of the Code of Canon Law teaches:

> “The evangelical counsel of chastity assumed for the Kingdom of Heaven, as a sign of the world to come and a source of more abundant fruitfulness in a heart not divided, entails the obligation to observe perfect continence in celibacy.”

The vow of chastity is not a simple abstention, but a **way of loving as Christ loved**. Whoever professes it commits to live with a heart totally given to God, directing all their affective capacity toward Him and toward the service of others.

In a society where love is measured by desire or utility, consecrated chastity reminds us that **true love does not possess, but gives itself**. It is the love that does not demand, but welcomes; that does not use, but **frees**.

> “Chaste love shows modern men and women a path of healing from isolation, in a form of loving that is free and liberating.”  
> — _Pope Francis_

The consecrated person lives chastity not as repression, but as an **anticipation of heaven**, where “they will no longer marry, but will be like the angels of God” (Mt 22:30). In their heart beats the eternal love of the Divine Spouse, a love that **embraces everyone without dividing**.

* * *

### 💧 The vow of poverty: free to love

Canon 600 indicates:

> “The evangelical counsel of poverty, following Christ who, being rich, became poor for us, entails besides an actually poor life and of spirit, a dependence and limitation in the use and disposition of goods according to the proper law of each institute.”

Living the evangelical poverty does not mean despising material goods, but **ordering them according to love**. The religious renounces ownership, not because goods are evil, but because they want **their only treasure to be God**.

In a world that idolizes consumption and comfort, consecrated poverty reminds us that **“man shall not live by bread alone” (Lk 4:4)**. It is a silent protest against selfishness and a proclamation of inner freedom.

Being poor for love is being able to say: _“My wealth is Christ”_. It is living detached, supportive, generous. It is not emptiness, but a **full availability to serve** and to share.

> “Poverty shows how things have value in the order of love, and rejects everything that can obscure its beauty: selfishness, greed, dependence.”  
> — _Pope Francis_

* * *

### 🔥 The vow of obedience: to listen and follow Christ

Canon 601 says:

> “The evangelical counsel of obedience, assumed in a spirit of faith and love in following Christ obedient unto death, obliges to submit the will to legitimate superiors when they command in accordance with the constitutions of one’s own institute.”

Obedience is perhaps the most demanding vow, because it touches the deepest part of the human person: their freedom. But it is also the one that **most transforms the soul into Christ**.

Jesus himself was “obedient unto death, even death on a cross” (Phil 2:8). The consecrated person learns from Him to trust, to listen, to renounce oneself out of love. To obey is not to submit blindly, but to **recognize the voice of God** in the mediation of the Church and of the superiors.

> “Obedience is a sign for our society because it is based on listening to one another and then acting, even at the cost of renouncing one’s own tastes and preferences.”  
> — _Pope Francis_

In a culture that exalts autonomy and “I do what I want,” the vow of obedience proclaims a forgotten truth: **true freedom is doing God’s will**.

* * *

### A love that becomes community

Vows are not lived in solitude. Each consecrated man and woman belongs to a **community**, where faith, prayer and mission are shared. It is a space where one learns to love concretely: in fraternal life, patience, forgiveness, service.

The religious does not seek only their own sanctification, but **builds together with others a spiritual family**. The community thus becomes the visible face of the Kingdom of God, where all are brothers and sisters in Christ.

In a world thirsty for authenticity, religious men and women are **living signs of hope**, witnesses that it is worth giving everything for love.

**Following Christ poor, chaste and obedient does not impoverish life… it fills it with meaning.**

## **Discerning Priestly Celibacy**

Are some of these thoughts yours regarding celibacy?

*   “I really like women!”
*   “I haven’t always lived a chaste life. Can I still be considered for the seminary?”
*   “I struggle with purity, so I’m not sure I have the holiness necessary to commit to celibacy.”
*   “Celibacy seems like a life of loneliness… will I be happy being alone?”
*   “I think I still want to be a father.”

The requirement of celibacy is, without a doubt, one of the greatest sources of anxiety and fear for a man discerning the priesthood. This is especially true in a society and culture saturated with sex.

The message we receive from the media and culture is very clear: no one can be happy and fulfilled without a lot of sexual activity. But this simply is not true.

As Fr. Benedict Groeschel wrote:

> “The media proclaim the message that sex brings happiness. If this were true, we would live in an earthly paradise and the world would be a ‘happy valley.’”

The good news is that God’s grace can achieve everything. By the power of Jesus’ cross, a man can overcome sexual lust and live in peace within his vocation. It can be done. It is possible. There is much evidence.

For example, there are approximately **four hundred thousand Catholic priests worldwide.** The vast majority of them, at some point, thought or said things like those mentioned earlier. Well, those four hundred thousand are now priests.

**God will never send us to a place where His grace cannot sustain us.**

Even if you struggle with chastity today, God offers you the grace to become sexually pure. Don’t let a concern about celibacy prevent you from considering the priesthood.

Above all, it is important to understand that priestly celibacy **is not about repressing sexuality**, but about proclaiming that the greatest joys of humanity are not found in earthly goods, but in union with God, in this life and in the eternal.

* * *

### The celibacy in Sacred Scripture

**Renouncing family:**

> “And everyone who has left houses, brothers, sisters, father, mother, children or lands for my name’s sake will receive a hundredfold and will inherit eternal life.” (Matthew 19:29)

**Freedom to serve:**

> “Are you free from a wife? Do not seek to marry... Those who marry will have troubles in the flesh, and I would spare you; but the unmarried man cares for the things of the Lord, how to please the Lord. But the married man cares about the things of the world, how to please his wife, and is divided.” (1 Corinthians 7:27-34)

**Celibacy for the Kingdom:**

> “Not all can receive this word, but only those to whom it is given. For there are eunuchs who were born that way, and there are eunuchs who were made eunuchs by others, and there are eunuchs who made themselves eunuchs for the sake of the kingdom of heaven. Let the one who can receive this receive it.” (Matthew 19:11-12)

The emphasis is on the special character of celibacy: not all men are suited for it, but it is a vocation that gives glory to the “Kingdom of God.”

* * *

### Frequently asked questions about celibacy

**Is dating allowed while in the seminary?** The seminary is like the engagement period for a couple: you don’t date others if you want to build a true relationship with the chosen person. Similarly, to truly prepare and discern the call to the priesthood in the seminary, one should not date.

**And if I have been sexually active in the past? Does that mean I cannot be a priest?** No. But now you must be in the process of embracing chastity. St. Augustine led a very disordered life in his youth, but he abandoned his impure ways when he decided to live fully as a Catholic. There should be a significant period of “sexual sobriety” before entering the seminary, normally at least two years.

**I am afraid I won’t be able to remain chaste.** If you ask God for it, He will give you abundant graces to live a chaste life. You must respond to those graces by making chaste decisions. As you grow in chastity and it becomes a habit of your life, you will experience strength and ease in living it. Celibacy is a serious commitment that must be at the center of discernment; it is not for everyone, but it is possible for those who are called.

**It seems unnatural to me to live my whole life without sex.** Most men and women are naturally called to marriage. Therefore, living a chaste and celibate life goes beyond the ordinary; it is, in fact, a supernatural call from God to live a radical love for the Church. Yes, it is a sacrifice, but the rewards are great. Throughout the centuries, many saints, religious, monks, nuns and priests have lived very full and happy lives.

* * *

### Why priests cannot marry?

> “I am very impatient with some of the pragmatic arguments in favor of celibacy — that it frees time and allows focus on other things —. I prefer to see celibacy as an irrational, overflowing, poetic and symbolic expression of the enamored soul.” — Fr. Robert Barron

Latin Rite priests renounce their natural right to marriage “for the Kingdom of Heaven,” as Jesus taught His disciples (Mt 19:12). It is a gift from God that opens a man’s heart to embrace all of God’s children in a deep way. His healthy and holy inclination toward marriage and family is transformed into a **supernatural fatherhood**, which makes his ministry—if faithful—**extraordinarily fruitful.**

* * *

### Other spiritual realities that celibacy signifies

*   Celibacy marks the priest as a man **consecrated to the service of Christ and the Church.** It shows concretely that he is not simply someone who performs functions or holds an office, but that he has been transformed in his being by the sacrament of Orders.
*   Celibacy **configures the priest more closely to Christ**, the great High Priest, who renounced earthly marriage for the Kingdom and to unite more perfectly with his heavenly Bride, the Church.
*   It is fitting that the priest who offers this same Jesus in sacrifice to the Father manifests in his own person (though imperfectly) the purity and holiness of the immaculate Victim.
*   Celibacy **reminds us of heaven**, pointing to the coming of the Kingdom, when marriage will no longer exist.

Some eras were more fruitful and others less. But today the question arises: **Is ministerial priesthood really necessary?** The answer is clear: **Yes!**

Priests are needed so that Christ’s message and His presence in the Sacraments continue shaping the history of salvation in humanity and in the People of God of all times.

We cannot measure vocations by quantity compared to past decades. Complaining does nothing. What matters is **to look with the eyes of Christ**, to go out to evangelize and mission even small communities. Perhaps it is time to **restore small communities**, to be **leaven**, even if a small leaven. As Jesus reminds us: “The Kingdom of Heaven is like the yeast that a woman took and mixed with three measures of flour, until it fermented all of it” (Mt 13:33)

Each Christian, living in the world without losing their nature, attracts people to the Lord by their example and word.

### **Example and testimony transform lives** Many times social movements and cultural trends do not make an evangelical life easy, but that **should not prevent showing that the Christian life is the best heritage we can offer**. Example and testimony make an impact on those who observe us. This is how St. Augustine experienced it: > Si isti et istae, cur non ego?” (If these men and women did it, why not me?) It was the testimony of his companions that made him reflect, abandon a dissolute and superficial life, and joyfully embrace the evangelical life, becoming a priest and, with time, a Bishop.

Today the same happens: the testimony of life attracts vocations. Therefore we must encourage families, consecrated men and women, priests and all the faithful People of God to live the following of Jesus with radicality.

## **Choosing who to share your life with**

**Choosing who to share your life with** is one of the most important decisions a Christian can make.  
It is not only about **finding someone you like**, but about **discovering the person God calls you to love and serve for life**.

**Loving with God’s eyes** means looking beyond emotion and impulse, and **learning to decide with the heart and the mind enlightened by faith.**

### **Don’t let feelings blind you**

True love is not a tsunami of emotions that sweeps you away without thinking.  
In the early phases — attraction and infatuation — there is a strong emotional and hormonal charge that can cloud reason. It is normal, but you must let the wave subside to see clearly.

> **“When you ask yourself ‘Is this good for me?’, you are on the right path.”**  
> Not because love is calculation, but because mature love knows how to discern.

Falling in love is not enough: **you must decide to love.**  
Or, as we often say: you fall in love with your heart, but you choose with your head.

* * *

### **Don’t skip stages**

Today it seems that relationships work like in TV series: two people meet, have dinner, like each other… and everything rushes.  
But love **does not grow by acts of impulse.**

Sexuality is meant as the **language of conjugal love**, and when it is rushed, **it confuses.**  
The body promises what the soul has not yet decided to give.

> **“Sex can cloud discernment: it makes you believe there is unity when it has not yet been built.”**

Many engagements break up because **they never really got to know each other**, because they talked little and touched much.  
Therefore the advice remains valid and wise:  
**talk a lot, pray together and touch little.**

Engagement is **not a ‘mini-marriage’**: it is a time to **discern if this person is the one you want to share life with.**  
It is not only about having a good time, but about **discovering if together you can grow in holiness.**

* * *

### **Courtship: a school of love**

Christian courtship is a **school of love**.  
It is not about possession, but about **learning to give oneself, to respect, to understand.**

In it, one learns to move from **infatuation —which is feeling— to love —which is deciding—.**

It is the time to get to know each other deeply:

*   What values move you
    
*   How you live the faith
    
*   What dreams you share
    
*   How you react to pain or frustration
    

> **It is not enough that the other person is good: you must see how you are together.**

**Ask yourself:**

*   How do we act when there are disagreements?
    
*   Do we know how to ask forgiveness and give in?
    
*   Do we share the same faith and life project?
    
*   Do we help each other become better or do we wear each other down?
    
*   Do we love each other with freedom, without emotional dependence?
    

Christian love **does not seek the other’s perfection**, but **to walk together toward it.**

* * *

### **Look with the eyes of faith**

In discerning as a couple you must look beyond the superficial.  
**You do not build a home on beauty or charm, but on the soul.**  
Appearance passes; heart and faith remain.

First, make sure they are **really Christian.**  
Not only baptized, but **believing, practicing, someone who lives their faith** and wants to walk with you toward God.

> Many marriages suffer because they united without sharing the same faith, hoping the other would “change.”  
> **Love does not convert by itself: only grace and freedom do.**

Also look at **maturity**: how they live their family life, how they work, how they face difficulties, how they manage money, whether they are responsible, faithful and honest.

Don’t trust those who **promise much and live little.**  
Habits do not change by magic in marriage.

> **“Before you travel by land, pray; if by sea, pray twice; and if you are going to marry, pray three times.”**  
> — _Russian proverb_

Marriage is not built on a smile nor on a moment of tenderness, but on everything you are: **thoughts, dreams, wounds, hopes and faith.**

* * *

### **A shared life project**

Getting married is not simply “loving each other a lot.”  
It is **wanting to be spouses**, to form a **community of life open to children and to God.**

Therefore, courtship must be a **path of preparation**, a process in which one decides—with freedom and truth—whether that love can become a **sacrament.**

Don’t trust infatuations or haste.  
Nor appearance or attractiveness.  
Seek a love **solidly founded on faith, virtue and trust.**

**Choose with prayer.**  
Listen to those who love you: parents, priests, friends of faith.  Ask for advice, but above all **ask God for light.**  
He knows your heart better than anyone.

* * *

### **Love with God’s eyes**

**Loving with God’s eyes** is seeing the other as He sees them: with **truth, tenderness and demand.**  
It is **desiring the other’s good more than one’s own pleasure.**  
It is **deciding to love even when you do not feel like it**, and trusting that the feeling will return, purified and stronger.

> **“Human love is serious, great and holy.”**

Therefore it must be built on solid foundations:  
**prayer, chastity, sincerity, faith and the will to serve.**

**Choosing well is not being lucky:**  
it is **knowing how to look with a heart in grace.**

**Requirements to be a priest**

To become a Catholic priest, a man must meet three basic requirements:

1.  Have access to university.
    
2.  Complete **two years of Philosophy**.
    
3.  Complete **four years of Theology**.
    

* * *

### **A seminarian’s daily life**

### **A seminarian’s daily life**

In one word: **intense**, but also **full of life**.  
The demands of the priesthood are great, so the formation is rigorous… but amidst study and prayer there is **time to live together, laugh and share as brothers**.

In addition to graduate-level studies, seminarians:

*   Pray together at least twice a day.
    
*   Participate in **daily Mass**.
    
*   Meet with their **spiritual director**.
    
*   Carry out **pastoral internships** in local parishes.
    

And between all that, there are moments for **sports, gatherings, jokes in the dining hall and long talks among friends** that forge true fraternity.  
Because the seminary not only forms priests: **it forms brothers who learn to live in community, with joy and with Christ at the center**.

* * *

### **The four pillars of priestly formation**

Being a priest **is not a job**, but **a new identity**: to become _alter Christus_, another Christ.  
Therefore, the Church proposes rigorous formation in **four fundamental areas**:

1.  **Human formation:** to cultivate a personality that is a **bridge to Christ** and that allows one to be an effective spokesperson for the Church.
    
2.  **Spiritual formation:** to develop a **deep and mature relationship with Christ** through prayer and a virtuous life.
    
3.  **Intellectual formation:** to know thoroughly the **truths of the faith** and acquire the skills to teach them to others.
    
4.  **Pastoral formation:** to learn to be a true **shepherd of souls**, accompanying the faithful in their joys and sufferings.
English:en.El camino hacia el sacerdocio es una ver:
The path to the priesthood is a true adventure of grace: a **journey where the heart learns to listen, to serve and to love like Christ, the Good Shepherd**.  
In our seminary, each stage of formation has its own rhythm and beauty, helping each young man to grow in freedom, maturity and joyful dedication.

### **1. Propedeutic Stage**

### **Current challenges of the lay vocation**

Despite this universal vocation, **many baptized people have still not become fully aware of their belonging to the Church**. Many consider themselves Catholics, but do not experience the Church as **a home that transforms their life and surroundings**. This creates situations where Christian values are seen as something “optional” or cultural, instead of being **the foundation of their identity**.

As a result:

*   Professional, political, economic, scientific, artistic and media life **is not always guided by evangelical criteria**.
    
*   There is an **incoherence between professed faith and real commitment** in daily life.
    
*   The laity do not always receive **adequate accompaniment from pastors**, which makes it difficult to discover and mature their vocation.
    

* * *

### **Obstacles in lay formation and action**

Some challenges come from **attitudes internal to the Church**:

*   The persistence of a **clerical mentality**, which limits the initiative of the laity in evangelizing action.
    
*   The preferential dedication of many lay people to **intra-ecclesial tasks**, without projecting their faith toward society.
    
*   Deficiencies in **integral formation**, which prevent responding effectively to today's societal challenges.
    

These factors make a **deep rediscovery of the lay vocation** necessary. Being Christian is not just practicing religious duties: **it is having a vocation**, and being lay means **ordering all social life from within**, from the heart of current reality, with the light of the Gospel.

### **The permanent diaconate**

The **Second Vatican Council** restored the **permanent diaconate** (LG 29) and defined it as “a proper and permanent degree within the hierarchy”. It can be conferred on **married men** who receive the **sacrament of orders** in its **third degree**.

Deacons are **strengthened by the laying on of hands** that comes from the Apostles and are more closely united to the **service of the altar**, fulfilling their ministry with the **grace of the diaconate** (AG 16).

* * *

### **Ministry and functions**

The deacon is called to live diakonía —the **service**— that characterizes his vocation. His mission is threefold: **to serve the Word, the Liturgy and Charity**.

Among his functions are:

*   Administering the **sacraments of Baptism and Matrimony**.
*   **Assisting the priest** at the Eucharist, **proclaiming the Gospel** and **distributing Communion**, both in the church and to the sick.
*   **Preaching**, **giving catechesis** and **presiding at funerals**.
*   **Administering parishes** and coordinating works of charity.

The deacon does not replace the priest nor the lay person, but has **his own identity and mission**, within the single service to the People of God.

* * *

### **Gospel foundation**

The diaconate is supported by the **New Testament** and expresses Christ’s command on service:

> “I did not come to be served, but to serve” (cf. Lk 22:27).

Jesus presents himself as the **first deacon**, the servant par excellence.

In the **Acts of the Apostles**, the Twelve choose **seven men of good repute**, full of the Holy Spirit, to serve at the tables and help the needy (Acts 6:1-6). Among them are **Stephen**, the first martyr, and **Philip**, called “the evangelist” (Acts 21:8).

* * *

### **Throughout history**

From the earliest centuries, the diaconate accompanied the bishop closely and had great importance in ecclesial life. The deacon **Saint Lawrence**, patron and example, was administrator and almoner of the Church of Rome, a model of dedication and fidelity.

The **Second Vatican Council** recovered the diaconate as a stable ministry, with **its own identity and mission**, opening a new stage in the life of the Church.

* * *

### **Today**

The permanent diaconate continues to grow as **the response of the Holy Spirit** to the current needs of the Church. In our diocese, **three men** have received this ministry: **two married and one celibate**. Each one, from his state of life, lives the deacon’s motto:

> “To serve as Christ the servant”.

### Difficulties and breakups: when love also purifies

**Loving is not always easy.**  
Every true love goes through moments of trial, doubts, wounds or even breakups. But there —in what hurts— there can also be a call from God. Love, when authentic, not only brings happiness: it also purifies, teaches and transforms.

### The trials of love

In courtship differences, disappointments, fatigue or fear of the future arise. Sometimes one feels unreciprocated as expected, or that the relationship has grown cold. It's normal.  
Love is not a straight path, but a school where God teaches us to **love beyond ourselves**.

> “Love does not consist in gazing at each other, but in looking outward together in the same direction.”  
> —Antoine de Saint-Exupéry

Difficulties can be a mirror where we discover our weaknesses, our selfishness or our wounds. Instead of fleeing from them, it is an opportunity to grow, to learn to forgive and to trust more in God.

### When it's time to let go

Sometimes love is also purified in **renunciation**. There are relationships that are not meant to continue, and discerning this with sincerity and prayer is also an act of love.  
Breaking up does not always mean failing: it can be the most honest and courageous way to love. God does not bless every relationship, but the one that leads us to holiness and true self-giving.

**Letting go with peace** is recognizing that the other belongs to God before us, and that happiness is not measured by holding on, but by loving in freedom.

> “To love is to will the good of the other, even if that good does not include me.”

### Healing with faith

After a breakup, wounds, feelings of guilt or emptiness may remain. But the heart is not made to stay broken: **God can heal** what seemed lost.  
It is a time of silence, prayer and accompaniment. Of letting grace repair what human love could not achieve.

The sacraments, spiritual direction and friendship are medicine. The Eucharist sustains, confession frees, prayer comforts. It is not only about “turning the page”, but about **letting God write a new one**.

### Love that matures

The trials of love are not an obstacle, but a purification. Mature love is born from pain embraced with faith. When it gives itself, forgives and learns, the heart expands and loves better.

Therefore, even breakups can be part of the vocational path: they help to know oneself, to purify desires and to prepare to love like Christ, with truth and without fear.

### To live it

*   Do not be afraid to ask for help: talking with a priest or a spiritual companion can clarify a lot.
    
*   Do not idealize or isolate yourself: Christian courtship is a path of freedom, not of dependence.
    
*   Do not extinguish hope: if God allowed a wound, it is because He wants to draw from it a greater love.
English:en.La vocación es el compromiso profundo de:
Vocation is the deep commitment to follow God's call. It requires effort and care to truly understand that call. This process of discovering God's will is known as **vocational discernment**.

Proper discernment involves several key elements:

*   **Deep self-knowledge:** understanding your personality, your strengths and weaknesses, your inclinations, your spirituality, your mental capacities and even your physical health.
    
*   **A solid knowledge of and sincere love for our Catholic faith.**
    
*   **Familiarity with the different vocations**, what they imply and the way of life they shape in those who embrace them.
    

Naturally, this process does not happen overnight. Vocational discernment is a **path** that can take months or even years. It requires study, prayer and, above all, patience.

*   Discernment **is not something that can be done in solitude**. The best way to discern is with the guidance of the Church, ideally accompanied by a priest or a trusted spiritual director who helps you discover where God may be calling you.
    
*   If you seek guidance —whether you have simple questions or need deeper accompaniment—, **we are here to help you!**

### Courtship as a vocation and a path of self-giving

**Courtship is not a parenthesis in Christian life, but a true call to love like Christ.**  
Just as marriage is a vocation to unconditional self-giving, courtship is a time of discernment and maturation in love. It is the stage where two people get to know each other, discover one another and prepare to decide if they want to give themselves to each other forever.

### A time of discernment and grace

Every Christian is called to holiness —including fiancés—. This time is not a pause, but an opportunity to grow in faith and virtue. Living courtship with God at the center means letting Him give meaning to the relationship: illuminating affections, purifying intentions and making love fruitful.

When a love draws you closer to God and helps you love others better, there is a Christian courtship. The more engaged couples love each other, the more capable they are of loving God, and vice versa.

> “The heart was created to love. Let us, then, put Christ in all our loves.”

### Learning to love

To love is not just to feel, but to learn to give oneself. Courtship is a school of love where virtues are forged: respect, patience, generosity and fidelity. Small gestures —listening, yielding, waiting— prepare for a love that lasts.

It is also a time to **form and grow together**. Reading, dialoguing, sharing concerns about faith and marriage helps to build on rock. It is important to be accompanied, seek advice and learn from those who have already walked that path.

### Living love with tenderness

An authentic love cares and respects. Chastity is not a denial of love, but its protection. It teaches to love without using, to wait to give oneself fully, to discover the beauty of the beloved person as a gift. Christian courtship is not measured by the intensity of desire, but by the depth of respect and the truth of the commitment.

> Loving is helping the other to become holy, not being an obstacle on their way to God.

### Joy, friendship and mission

Courtship is also a time of **friendship, laughter and shared life**. It is not about closing in on the relationship, but about opening up together to the world: serving, doing apostolate, living the faith with joy. A Christian couple not only loves: **is a testimony of God's love in the world.**

### The power of the sacraments

Couples who pray together, who go to Mass, who confess, who put God at the center, experience that their love becomes stronger and freer. In the sacraments one finds the grace to forgive, to understand and to grow in communion.

Courtship is, ultimately, **a vocation to true love**, an invitation to learn to love as Christ loves his Church: with patience, tenderness and self-giving.

### **The first home of vocation: the family**

Every vocation begins at home. Not in a seminary, nor in a convent, but **in the warmth of a family that prays, loves and serves**.  
There one learns to say “yes”, to look beyond oneself, to discover that life becomes great when it is given away.

*   The family is the **first seminary of the heart**.
    
*   Where one is taught to **speak with God naturally**.
    
*   Where one learns that faith **is not theory, but shared life**.
    

### **The community: cradle where the call grows**

No one discerns alone.  
The **parish community**, the group, the movement, are places where faith becomes a living experience.  
There one **discovers their gifts, shares concerns and finds concrete models** of self-giving.

👉 The community does not replace God's voice, but **helps to recognize it**.  
👉 It accompanies, encourages, supports… and **prays**.

> _A community that prays for vocations, makes them be born._

### **A Church of vocations**

We need families and communities that **live their own vocation with joy**, knowing that this is already a testimony.  
When a marriage lives united, when a priest serves with passion, when a religious sister smiles with faith, **they are preaching with their life**.

### **Sowing vocations in our environments**

Vocation is not a topic of the past nor only for “others”.  
It is the **great adventure of every Christian**: discovering how God wants to love the world through you.

🌾 **Parents, catechists, priests, friends…**  
Let us speak of vocation naturally.  
Let us look at our young people with eyes of faith:

> “This boy would make a good priest.”  
> “That girl has a big heart for serving.”

And not only think it: **let us pray for them**.  
Every prayer is a seed in God’s field.

English:en.## **La familia: Iglesia doméstica**\n\n:
## **The family: domestic Church**

Christ wanted to be born and grow in the Holy Family of Joseph and Mary. From its origins, the family has been **the first nucleus of Christian life**, where faith is taught, lived and transmitted. Every believing home is a **domestic Church**, a place where God's love is proclaimed first through mutual self-giving and daily example.

* * *

### Fathers and mothers, first evangelizers

Parents are the **first preachers of the faith**. With their words and above all with their example, they teach their children to live in God.  
They foster vocations and help to discover each family member's personal call. Holiness is learned at home, in patience, forgiveness, work and daily prayer.

**Suggested image:** Parents reading the Bible to their children, showing closeness and unity.

* * *

#### **A community of faith, hope and charity**

The Christian family is **a communion of persons**, which reflects the communion that exists in God among Father, Son and Holy Spirit.  
Through prayer, the sacraments and daily life, the members exercise **the baptismal priesthood**, offering their life as a sign of love and self-giving. Here one learns to be generous, patient and to love without reserve.

**Suggested image:** Family praying together, in an attitude of recollection.

* * *

### Image of God the Creator

As God creates and educates, the family participates in his work: **to procreate, educate and form in love**. Every home is **an image of God**, responsible for transmitting life, love and hope. The family mission begins by first proclaiming God's love among its members, in daily self-giving and mutual care.

**Suggested image:** Family embraced in a natural landscape, reflecting love and creation.

* * *

#### A mission that lights up the world

Living the faith in family is not only caring for one's own home, it is **being a beacon for others**. Daily acts of love and service teach children and show those around us that Christian life is true and beautiful. The family evangelizes with its example, commitment and self-giving.

**Suggested image:** Family participating in parish activities or community service.

* * *

### Prayer and daily life

Family prayer **unites and strengthens**. Reading the Word of God, praying together and putting God at the center of daily life makes a difference in decisions, behaviors and affective bonds.  
If the home revolves only around the worldly, the sacred dimension of life is lost. A family that prays stays united and transmits faith.

**Suggested image:** Family praying before a meal or in a daily moment of union.

* * *

## **Dignity and responsibility**

The Christian family is **a living Church present in the world**, a reflection of God's love. Each member has the dignity and responsibility to **proclaim first by life and self-giving to the other**. The home not only lives the faith, it radiates it; it forms, accompanies and evangelizes. Being a Christian family is **a call to love without limits, to overcome selfishness and to live total self-giving**, as God loves us.

**Suggested final image:** Collage of Christian families in prayer, celebrations and service, showing unity and diversity.

1.  What does a priest do?  
    The purpose of a priest is to bring people to Jesus and Jesus to the people. He does this primarily by preaching the Word and offering the Sacrifice of the Mass.

His daily life consists of administering the sacraments —Baptism, Confirmation, Eucharist, Penance and Reconciliation, Anointing of the Sick and Marriage (Holy Orders is administered by the bishop)— and attending to the spiritual and human needs of his community.

* * *

2.  What exactly is a “vocation”?  
    A vocation is a call from God to do something specific for Him and for His Kingdom. The primary vocation of every person is to be holy: to love and serve God, obey his commandments and cooperate with Christ in the work of redemption by loving and serving others.

But we are all also called to a secondary vocation, a “state of life” in which we must be holy.

* * *

3.  What are those “secondary vocations” I might be called to?  
    Many people are called to marriage, but it is an error to assume that is automatically your vocation. You may also be called to the priesthood, to religious life as a brother or sister, or to the diaconate.

Finally, some follow Christ in the state of life of celibacy. Remember: it is normal to desire marriage and family. That desire does not exclude that you may have a priestly vocation.

* * *

4.  How can I know what God is calling me to?  
    You should pray every day asking God to reveal his plan to you. Do not ask yourself: “What do I want to do when I grow up?”, but: “Jesus, what do You want me to do?”. And listen for the answer!

The main place where God speaks is the heart. Listen with your heart. Also, discernment for the priestly vocation is always done with the Church. The local bishop, assisted by the vocational office and the seminary, is who finally confirms the call.

* * *

5.  Can I be happy if I do not follow the plan God has for me?  
    If you do not follow the vocation for which you were created, you can achieve a certain happiness in this life and still be saved, but you will never be as fully happy as if you followed your true vocation.

That is why it is so important to discern correctly. Of course in every vocation there are trials and difficulties, but also great joy in giving your life for Jesus.

* * *

6.  Are most priests happy in their vocation?  
    Most priests are very happy! Priestly life is deeply rewarding, both in this life and in eternity.

The media sometimes give a distorted image of priests, portraying them as frustrated or unhappy, or reducing them to the scandals of a few. That simply is not true.

* * *

7.  Why can't priests marry? Isn't that very difficult?  
    Priests of the Roman Rite do not marry in order to devote themselves completely to Jesus and to his people. They beget “spiritual children” by bringing many souls to Christ and helping them grow in holiness.

Celibacy is a powerful sign to the world that only Jesus can give us the happiness we all long for. Renouncing marriage and family shows that Christ is real and worthy of giving one's life for Him.

Every vocation demands sacrifices, but there is great joy in sacrificing out of love. As one priest said: “It is true that no one will call me ‘dad’, but thousands call me ‘father’.”

* * *

8.  Will priests ever be allowed to marry?  
    Celibacy will always exist in the Church because it is not just a law, but a charism, a spiritual gift and a source of fruitfulness. Jesus was celibate. Saint Paul too.

Celibacy helps the priest unite more intimately with Christ and be a sign of the Kingdom of God. Although there are some married priests in the Catholic Church, they are exceptional cases.

If the Holy Spirit ever willed a change, it would be carried out through the Pope and the bishops. But it would be a serious mistake to enter the seminary “hoping” that this would happen.

* * *

9.  Would there be more priests if they could marry?  
    Perhaps, but the question is whether that would be best for the Church. Celibacy for the Kingdom is a powerful testimony that Jesus is real and worthy of total self-giving.

Moreover, priestly vocations have grown greatly in recent decades in Africa, Asia and Latin America, while they have declined in Europe and the United States. The problem is not celibacy, but deeper cultural and social factors.

* * *

10.  Will I be alone if I become a priest?  
    Loneliness is part of every vocation, but priests are rarely alone: they accompany people at the most important moments of their lives —birth, sacraments, marriage, death— and live surrounded by their community.

When loneliness arrives, Jesus fills that void, as He does in every vocation.

* * *

11.  Do priests receive a salary?  
    Yes, although they live simply. They receive what is necessary to cover their expenses, maintain a vehicle, rest and carry out normal activities. In addition, the parish provides their housing and food, so their expenses are minimal.

* * *

12.  Can priests have fun?  
    Of course. Priests can play sports, watch movies, read, travel, go to the theater, fish, play soccer or golf, as long as it is consistent with Christian life.

* * *

13.  If I am attracted to the priesthood, does that mean I have a vocation?  
    Possibly, but not necessarily. It is important to pray, go to Mass, live Christianly and talk with a priest or the vocational director. They can help you discern clearly.

* * *

14.  I'm not very “holy”. Can I still be a priest?  
    Yes. Holiness is a lifelong path. God forms his priests little by little. Use the sacrament of Confession, pray daily and you will see how Christ transforms you.

* * *

15.  Is it easy to become a priest?  
    No. Serious formation is required: four years of university (including philosophy) and another four in the seminary to obtain a master's degree in theology. But do not be discouraged: the seminary is a wonderful experience and God gives the necessary grace.

* * *

16.  Is so much education necessary?  
    Yes. The priest must be well formed in the humanities, theology and spiritual life to serve wisely and be respected by the faithful. Every soul is precious and deserves a prepared pastor.

* * *

17.  What qualities does the Church look for in a candidate?  
    He must be a practicing Catholic, who prays daily, lives the commandments, serves others, enjoys good physical, mental and emotional health, and has average or above-average intelligence. Above all, he must be open to God's will.

* * *

18.  If I enter the seminary “to try it out”, am I already committing for life?  
    No. The seminary is precisely the place to discern. Many men enter, try it for a time and later choose another path. And even so, they leave strengthened in their faith.

* * *

19.  Is the life of a priest interesting?  
    Very much! Each day is different. There are challenges, but also profound joy. At the end of the day, the priest can say: “Lord, today I have given myself for You”. There is no fuller way to live.

English:en.## **¿Cómo saber si Dios me llama? — Ven:
## **How to know if God is calling me? — Overcoming fear**

Perhaps the idea of the priesthood has crossed your mind at some time, but fear drives it away:

*   Fear of commitment
*   Fear of celibacy
*   Fear of not being worthy

These fears are very common, even among those already in the seminary. But literally thousands of men have had the same doubts and still went on to become holy and devoted priests.

The first truth you must remember is that **God does not speak through fear**. Fear is a weapon of the Enemy to turn you away from God’s will; it is like the bite of an animal that paralyzes its prey so it cannot move.

A man dominated by fear will have difficulty moving toward God’s will.

So, how to overcome fear? Here are **five ideas**:

* * *

### **1) Turn your fears into concerns.**

You may have legitimate concerns about celibacy or preaching, but that is not the same as being afraid. Instead of letting fear dominate you, look at the demands of the priesthood with objectivity. It is true that a priest needs self-control, affective maturity, and the ability to speak in public. These and other areas require a serious personal examination.

Yes, you will discover things you need to improve, but make your discernment with a calm mind, not with a frightened heart.

> “Perfect love drives out fear” (1 Jn 4:18).

Remember that when Jesus called Peter (Lk 5:1-11), the first Pope said to him:

> “Depart from me, Lord, for I am a sinful man.”

And Jesus assured him that he should not be afraid to follow him. In the same way, Jesus knows your weaknesses and difficulties. If you trust in Him and “cast your nets into the deep,” everything will be fine.

* * *

### **2) Reflect on God’s love.**

Fr. Brett Brannen, in his book Saving a Thousand Souls, recommends this meditation when a man feels fear:

> “God is infinite in power and loves me infinitely. No one can snatch me from his hand. God will never send me where his grace cannot sustain me. If he asks something difficult of me, like to be a priest, he will give me the grace to do it. I will not fail, because He is with me. I will be happy because I do his will. Even if I do not have all the necessary qualities, God will help me develop them. In his will is my peace.”

* * *

### **3) Entrust your fears to the Virgin Mary.**

Remember that after the angel told her “do not be afraid,” Mary promptly accepted God’s will:

> “Behold the handmaid of the Lord; be it done to me according to your word.”

Entrust your fears to her intercession: she will calm your heart and help you discover her Son’s will.

* * *

### **4) Remember what the seminary is for.**

From a practical point of view, it is consoling to know that if God calls you to the priesthood, ordination is still far off. The seminary is a time of intense formation to face doubts, grow in holiness, and prepare for a fruitful ministry. **No man enters the seminary already ready to be a priest.**

* * *

### **5) Seek solace in the Word of God.**

If you are afraid of the priesthood, you are not alone. Prophets and apostles also felt fear when they were called. Read the following biblical passages to see how God encouraged them:

*   **I am not holy enough:** Is 6:1-9; Lk 5:1-11
*   **I fear failure:** Ex 14:10-31; Lk 15
*   **I have sinned:** Jn 21:15-23; Mt 9:9-13; Lk 7:36-50
*   **I am too young:** 1 Sam 3:1-18; 1 Sam 16:1-13; Jer 1:4-10; Lk 1:26-38
*   **I do not have enough talent:** 1 Sam 17:32-51; Lk 1:26-38
*   **I want to have a family:** Gn 12:1-3; Mt 12:46-50; Mk 10:28-30
*   **I want “a good life”:** Mk 10:17-31; 1 Cor 2:9; Mt 13:44-46; Jn 10:10; Mt 16:24-27
*   **I am afraid to commit forever:** Ruth 1:15-17; Mt 28:16-20; 1 Cor 12:5-10
*   **I am scared to speak in public:** Ex 4:10-17; Jer 1:4-10
*   **I am not intelligent enough:** 2 Cor 4:7-18; Ex 4:10-17
*   **I fear being alone:** Ex 3:4-22; Lk 1:28-38; Mt 28:20
*   **I want to be happy:** Ps 37:4; Mt 5:1-12; Jn 10:10; Mk 10:28-31; 1 Cor 2:9
*   **I am full of fear:** 1 Jn 4:18 “There is no fear in love; perfect love drives out fear.”

As Saint John Paul II often reminded: **Do not be afraid!** Do not let fear paralyze you. Talk with a priest you trust about your concerns.

Remain faithful to daily prayer, trust in God and your heart will be at peace, whatever your vocation may be.

Every baptized faithful has a unique place in the history of salvation. Through their faith, dedication, and commitment, laity participate in Christ’s mission: **priestly, prophetic, and royal**, each according to their gifts and circumstances. ### **The heart of the lay vocation** Being lay does not mean being a spectator. ## **Not just pray, seek**

### **Vocation does not arise from nothing**

Sometimes it seems that vocations — to the priesthood, to marriage or to consecrated life — **arise from nothing**, as if God called in secret without anyone else having a part.  
But that is not so: **God calls through concrete faces, through living communities, through people who truly care.**  
Therefore, it is not enough to pray for vocations. **They must be sought.**

* * *

### **Pray yes… but with eyes open**

Jesus said it clearly: “The harvest is plentiful and the workers are few; therefore pray earnestly to the Lord of the harvest to send out workers into his harvest” (Mt 9:37-38).  
That prayer is not passive or theoretical. It is a call to **become ourselves collaborators of God**, those who help others discover their path.

Praying for vocations means **looking around**: at the young people of your parish, your friends, those who serve with joy, those who listen patiently, those who live the faith coherently.  
When you see someone like that, **do not remain silent**. Perhaps it is time to ask, simply and confidently:

> “Have you ever thought that God might be calling you to something more?”

Sometimes a question like that, asked by a **priest**, a **catechist** or a **believing friend**, can awaken a sleeping vocation.

* * *

### **Each one seeks the holiness of the other**

Vocation is not a private matter. **We are all responsible for one another’s holiness.**  
A layperson who encourages, a mother who prays, a priest who proposes, a community that accompanies… all participate in the birth of new vocations.

The world needs **good husbands**, **good priests**, **good consecrated women**. And that begins when someone dares to look with faith at another’s qualities:

> “He would be a devoted father.”  
> “She could be a great sister.”  
> “He has a shepherd’s soul.”

It is not about labeling, but about **recognizing God’s action** in people and helping them discern it.

* * *

### **Point, accompany, pray**

Look carefully. **Write down in your heart** the names of those who convey joy, hope, service.  
Accompany them with your friendship, your prayer, your example.  
And pray each day:

> “Lord, make each one discover their path, and help us to accompany each other in discernment.”

* * *

### **A vocation that is born in community**

No vocation flourishes in solitude. **It arises in a community that prays, listens, and walks together.**  
Synodality — that walking together — is not just a pastoral method: **it is the very way God calls**.  
Every vocation, every story, is the fruit of a people that accompanies, proposes and sustains.

### **The harvest is plentiful**

Jesus said it truly: **there is much work to do and few hands willing to do it.**  
Souls —that is the harvest— **are waiting for shepherds to accompany them, to heal them, to lead them to God.**  
But if priests are lacking, **those who bring the Gospel, who celebrate the sacraments, who announce Christ’s forgiveness and mercy, are missing.**

It is not only a numerical shortage: it is an **urgency of the heart of the Church.**  
There is a hunger for God, a thirst for meaning, a need for shepherds.  
And Christ himself has told us how to respond: **by asking.**

* * *

### **A call to pray**

Jesus did not say “organize more” or “seek better methods.” He said:

> **“Ask the Lord of the harvest.”**

Priestly vocation **does not arise from a strategy, but from prayer.**  
God continues to call, but **He expects His people to intercede.**  
When the Church prays, the Holy Spirit acts; when a family prays, a heart can hear the call.

Therefore, **every Christian has a real responsibility:**  
**to ask the Lord of the harvest to send holy, generous, joyful workers.**

* * *

### **Pray with perseverance**

It is not enough to ask once. Jesus spoke of **praying without losing heart.**  
Priestly vocations are born in a Church that **prays with insistence and trust.**

Pray each day, pray as a family, pray the Rosary asking for priests and for those who could become priests.  
**Each Hail Mary is a seed.**  
And how many priests, when recounting their story, confess it:

> “My grandmother used to pray the Rosary for vocations.”  
> “A group in my parish prayed every week for new priests.”  
> “Someone, in silence, was praying for me.”

**Nothing is lost.** Every prayer moves the heart of God.

* * *

### **The generosity of interceding**

Asking for vocations is an act of faith, but also of generosity.  
It means recognizing that **the Church does not belong to us**: it belongs to Christ.  
And He wants His harvest to have workers, His people to have shepherds.

Dedicating time, prayer, sacrifice, even offering a Rosary or a Communion for vocations, **is part of our mission as laity, families and communities.**  
There is no prayer more fruitful than one that asks for those who will one day **bring God’s grace to so many souls.**

* * *

### **A Church that prays united**

Vocation is born in a **community that prays**, that walks united, that lives the **synodality** of being responsible for everyone.  
It is not enough to wait for “others” to pray.  
**Each one matters.** Each one can be an instrument so that a young man hears the voice of Christ calling:

> “Come and follow me.”

* * *

### **Ask with faith**

The harvest is plentiful. Souls wait.  
And the Lord has given us the way: **ask, trust, insist.**

Ask each day the Lord of the harvest.  
Do it with faith, with constancy, with love for the Church.  
Because God listens. And when the Church prays, **He answers.**

## What do nuns do?

### Two paths, the same gift: active life and contemplative life

When someone asks “what do nuns do?”, the most honest answer would be:  
**“they love, serve and pray for the world.”**  
But behind those three words there is **a whole life of dedication.**  
Some do it **in silence, behind walls**, and others **in the midst of the noise of the world.**  
Both ways are two faces of the same love: **Christ**.

> “Nuns are the feminine face of a Church that prays, serves and loves.”

* * *

## Cloistered nuns: the hidden heart that supports everyone

They are the **contemplative nuns**, those who live “hidden with Christ in God.”  
From the silence of their monasteries, **they pray for everyone**, for believers and non-believers, for those who suffer, for those who love, for the whole world.

### This is how their day beats

Their life is marked by a serene and constant rhythm:

*   **Personal prayer** from dawn.
    
*   **Eucharist** as the center of everything.
    
*   **Manual work**: garden, sewing, sweets, icons…
    
*   **Silence**, which is not emptiness, but **encounter with God**.
    
*   **Spiritual reading** and moments of community.
    

> “Silence does not separate them from the world, it unites them to it from within.”

Although they live in cloister, **they are not disconnected**.  
They welcome visitors in the parlor, pray for concrete intentions, and some produce goods they sell to support their community.  
In a world that runs, they **pause so that love keeps breathing**.

* * *

## Active life nuns: the visible hands of the Gospel

While the contemplatives pray in silence, the **active life nuns** go out to meet the world.  
They are the ones who **teach, care for, accompany, heal and evangelize**.  
Their prayer becomes **action**, their cloister is the **heart of the neighbor**.

You will find them:

*   In **schools and universities**, forming minds and hearts.
    
*   In **hospitals**, caring for the sick with tenderness.
    
*   In **poor neighborhoods**, sharing life with the poorest.
    
*   In **distant missions**, proclaiming Christ with a smile.
    
*   In **parishes**, accompanying groups, young people, families, the elderly.
    

> “While some pray for the world, others embrace it with their hands. But both love it with the same love.”

* * *

## Two paths, one love

Although they live in different ways, **all nuns have the same mission**:  
**to follow Christ more closely and make his love present.**  
Some do it from contemplation; others, from action.  
But both are **invisible pillars** that support the body of the Church.

> “If the Church is a body, cloistered nuns are the heart that prays,  
> and active nuns are the hands that serve.”

The contemplatives remind that God is the center.  
The active remind that **God’s love is translated into works**.  
And together they teach us that **faith is not understood without prayer nor without charity**.

* * *

## 💬 Why choose such a life?

Because in a world that seeks success, they choose **to give their lives**.  
In a time of noise, **they choose silence or service**.  
And in a society that runs without direction, **they stop to look at Christ**.

Being a nun —cloistered or active— is **a vocation of radical love**:  
a total “yes” to God, a lifelong commitment to the Gospel.

> “It does not matter if they pray or teach, if they cook or mission:  
> everything in them shouts that God is worth the whole life.”

* * *

## Two styles, the same melody

In monasteries or in the streets,  
in silence or among the cries of the world,  
**nuns remain witnesses that God is alive**.

And while the world runs seeking meaning,  
they —with prayer or action— remind us of the deepest secret:  
**happiness is in giving oneself completely.**

**A Sacred Ministry to the People of God** _"The faithful expect only one thing from priests: that they be specialists in promoting the encounter between man and God. They are not asked to be experts in economics, construction or politics. They are expected to be experts in spiritual life."_ ~ Pope Benedict XVI

**Could God be calling you to be a priest?** God made you for a unique purpose. Even before you were born, He knew your vocation, your mission in life. And if you are a faithful Catholic man, God could be calling you to a higher purpose: to become a Catholic priest.

Priests have a crucial mission: to bring people to Jesus and to bring Jesus to people. They are spiritual fathers to thousands of Catholics. They preach the Gospel and offer the sacrifice of the Mass. In short, priests are living witnesses of Christ in the world: men of firm character who stand out in our secular culture.

A good priest is a spiritual hero, a man who sacrifices himself for the people of God. Is Jesus calling you to be his priest?

**The priesthood is a vocation.** Christ asks some men for the sacrifice of their lives to follow him as his closest companions. From all eternity, certain men are called to the priesthood.

It is a call written into their nature and, therefore, a call that will bring them fulfillment.

**A priest acts In Persona Christi.** Priests act _in persona Christi capitis_, which means “in the person of Christ, head of the Church.” That is why the priest speaks in the first person at Mass: “This is my body, given for you.”

**A priest possesses a Sacred Power.** When a priest makes the sacraments present, he possesses a sacred power granted by God, in Latin, _sacra potestas_.

**A priest’s soul changes forever.** At ordination, a man’s soul undergoes an ontological change—a change of being—that marks his soul indelibly forever. Once a priest, always a priest.

## What is Christian courtship?

Courtship is a time to **get to know each other, interact and respect one another**. It is not a mere stage before marriage, but an opportunity to learn to love truly. The Church invites living it deeply and joyfully, because it is the natural path to discern the vocation to conjugal love and to prepare for a total and faithful giving.

* * *

## Getting to know each other: discovering the other to love them better

Courtship is a time of mutual knowledge. In it, two people discover each other little by little: their character, their dreams, their faith, their way of facing life. Whoever has been called by God to marriage needs to know well the person with whom he or she will share life. The greater the knowledge, the lower the risk of making a mistake.

Therefore, the Church wishes that before marriage there be a time of courtship, to get to know one another more and thus love each other better. This knowledge is not reduced to external data, but implies discovering the other’s heart: their faith, values, wounds and virtues.

Loving is not letting oneself be carried away only by feeling. True love integrates **feeling, intellect and will**. Feeling ignites, intellect illuminates and will sustains. Love is not improvised: it is learned, cultivated and chosen each day.

* * *

## Interacting: sharing life with sincerity and faith

One cannot know without interaction, nor love without sharing. The interaction between engaged couples must be deep and sincere, covering essential topics: faith, vision of family, children, work, values… Engagement cannot be based on appearances or fleeting emotions, but on the search for the other’s truth.

Christian couples relate to each other with respect and patience, knowing that both are fragile and that love requires forgiveness and understanding. It is not about waiting for the other to change, but learning to love them as they are, and discerning whether both walk in the same direction.

Interaction also implies recognizing if there is **affective maturity**. Immaturity shows when someone lives guided by moods, cannot wait, needs attention or fears commitment. A Christian courtship helps to grow in self-mastery, to give space to the other and to cultivate a free and sincere relationship.

* * *

## Respecting each other: loving with purity and freedom

Respecting one another is recognizing that the other is a gift, not a possession. Mutual respect is expressed in delicacy, temperance and chastity. Chastity is not a denial of love, but its noblest defense: it protects the heart and teaches to love without using the other.

Pope Francis reminds that courtship is “a time of waiting and preparation, to be lived in the chastity of gestures and words.” That waiting strengthens love, makes it free, mature and capable of total giving. One cannot build a forever love on the pursuit of immediate pleasure.

Respecting each other also means caring for communication, avoiding emotional blackmail and not putting the other in extreme situations. Authentic love always seeks the good of the beloved, not one’s own satisfaction. Thus one learns to love as Christ loved: with patience, with giving and without expecting anything in return.

* * *

## The three phases of love

We can say that human love has three phases, which do not replace but integrate each other:

1.  **Attraction:** it arises spontaneously. Someone seems attractive; interest and the desire to know arise.
    
2.  **Falling in love:** feelings are on edge. One enjoys the other’s presence and dreams of a future together.
    
3.  **Decided love:** it is the most mature phase. Loving is no longer only feeling, but **wanting to love**: deciding to do so each day, even when it is hard.
    

Feeling is not chosen, but love is. Loving is a decision that implies sacrifice, fidelity and will. When one loves this way, feeling returns stronger and deeper, because gratuitous love —given without expecting anything in return— generates joy and fulfillment.

* * *

## A path toward true love

Christian courtship is a path to learn to love like Christ: with freedom, tenderness and giving. It is not about seeking perfection, but walking together toward it, supported by God’s grace.

Living such a courtship is preparing the foundations of a solid marriage. As Pope Francis says, _“living together is an art, a patient, beautiful and fascinating path that has rules summarized in three words: May I?, Thank you, Sorry.”_  
Three words that also summarize a holy courtship: respect, gratitude and constant reconciliation.

## What does a monk do?

**Ora et labora** —pray and work—.  
That is the formula that sums up the whole life of the monk. But behind those three words there is a world: a way of life centered on **the search for God**, in the silence of the monastery and in the peace of a routine offered as prayer.

* * *

### A life centered on God

The **monk** lives to **contemplate God**. He does not flee the world, but embraces it from the heart, interceding for the needs of all people.  
Each day, his prayer invisibly sustains the Church.  
His vocation is **contemplative**, but not useless: monks draw grace upon the world with their faithful silence.

* * *

### The day’s rhythm: prayer, reading and work

The monk’s day turns like a sacred clock around three axes:

1.  **Prayer** – communal and personal.  
    Monks pray the **Divine Office**, the liturgical “hours” that mark the day:
    
    *   **Matins or Vigils**, at dawn.
        
    *   **Lauds**, to offer the day.
        
    *   **Terce, Sext and None**, during work.
        
    *   **Vespers**, at evening.
        
    *   **Compline**, before rest.
        
    
    And at the center of everything: the **Eucharist**, the living heart of the monastery.

    
2.  **Lectio divina** – the prayerful reading of the Word.  
    It is not academic study, but **listening to the Spirit**. From it arose the great Benedictine libraries that preserved Christian and Greco-Roman culture for centuries.

    
3.  **Work** – manual or intellectual, always offered to God.  
    In an abbey, there may be bakers, shoemakers, gardeners, bookbinders, musicians, librarians or teachers.  
    Everything is done in obedience, in silence and with love.

    

* * *

### Ora et labora: a prayer made work

In the monastery **there are no empty hours**. Everything —singing the psalms, repairing a shoe or copying a book— is a form of prayer.  
Work supports the monastery and enables works of charity.  
The balance between prayer, work and study keeps the monk **in peace, serene and centered on God**.

* * *

### The great guardians of culture

From the loving attention to **lectio divina**, monks naturally moved to **study**.  
Therefore, medieval abbeys were **beacons of light** in dark times:  
they copied manuscripts, taught reading and sowed the foundations of European culture.

* * *

### A communal life, not solitary

Although “monk” comes from the Greek _monos_ (alone), the monk **does not live in isolation**, but **in community**.  
Under the guidance of an abbot, all seek “**to have one heart and one soul in God**”, as Saint Augustine says.  
The monastery is a family where each brother helps the other to reach heaven.

* * *

### Not all religious are monks

**Monks** live according to the **Rule of Saint Benedict**, centered on contemplation.  
**Friars** (Franciscans, Dominicans, Carmelites…) also consecrated, go out into the world to preach and serve.  
And **religious clerics** (like the Jesuits) devote their lives to apostolate and teaching.  
Each path is different, but all seek the same: **God in all things**.

* * *

### In the words of Saint Benedict

> “Put nothing before the love of Christ.”  
> — _Rule of Saint Benedict, ch. 4_

**Priests do much more than celebrate Mass and pray all day.**  
The life of a priest is active, demanding, challenging… and deeply rewarding.

There are many specialized ministries, such as being a chaplain, working in archdiocesan offices or teaching in a seminary. But most priests serve in parishes.

The vast majority of priests live happy and fulfilling lives. They love the people they serve and, in turn, are loved by their parishioners. Traditionally, priests are considered to fulfill the biblical role of **priest, prophet and king.**

Priests guide, unite and encourage their faithful.

Priests administer the sacraments and foster holiness.

*   Welcoming new members into the Church through Baptism.
    
*   Hearing confessions and offering spiritual direction.
